variants.name: kotlinx.coroutines Mutex with withLock
variants.idiom_name: public suspend functions using mutex.withLock + private non-suspending helpers
variants.implementation_notes: kotlinx.coroutines' Mutex is documented as non-reentrant - invoking lock even from the coroutine that currently holds it suspends the invoker - so the interleaving hazard is real and the pattern's discipline is required in coroutine code. withLock is the scope-bound boundary for a public suspend function, and the internal helpers should be plain private functions that assume the mutex is held, never call a public suspending entry point, and never take the mutex again; if an internal step must suspend, keep it inside the same withLock and make sure it cannot call back into a locking public function. For thread-based JVM code the same component uses synchronized/@Synchronized instead, where reentrancy removes the deadlock force.
pitfalls: Mutex is non-reentrant by design: a nested withLock on the same mutex simply suspends the caller forever - no error, only a hang.
Holding a Mutex across suspension points is allowed but keeps other coroutines waiting inside the critical section; never call a blocking lock, Thread.sleep or runBlocking in a withLock body.
unlock() from a non-owner throws IllegalStateException, so only the acquiring coroutine may release (withLock does this for you).
Cancellation releases the mutex through withLock, but a helper that swallows CancellationException can keep working while another coroutine already owns the mutex.

variants.name: JVM monitors (@Synchronized / synchronized block)
variants.idiom_name: public synchronized functions + private unsynchronized helpers
variants.implementation_notes: On the JVM, Kotlin's synchronized blocks and @Synchronized functions compile to monitorenter/monitorexit on the receiver, and the JVM monitor is reentrant: intra-component calls re-acquire and only raise the hold count, so the deadlock half of the pattern is already absorbed. The remaining realization is the classic split - a public synchronized function acquires once and a private unsynchronized function assumes the monitor is held - which keeps hold counts at 1 and the critical section explicit. It is the natural choice for blocking, thread-based components; suspending code must not use it, because it blocks a dispatcher thread. Note that the common expect annotation kotlin.Synchronized is deprecated (warning since Kotlin 1.8, error since 2.1) because synchronization only exists on the JVM; use the synchronized { } stdlib function with an explicit lock object, or the JVM-specific kotlin.jvm.Synchronized.
pitfalls: The JVM monitor is reentrant, so a violation is silent - only the hold count and the length of the critical section reveal it.

@Synchronized locks the receiver instance (and the common expect annotation is deprecated); use a dedicated private lock object with synchronized(lock) { } so the component does not expose its monitor.
Blocking calls inside the monitor (I/O, database, another lock) serialise the component and can invert lock order; keep the body to in-memory mutation.
Never mix the monitor with a kotlinx.coroutines Mutex on the same component: the two locks do not exclude each other.
